en.g: in the hereafter; beyond the grave, in heaven or eternal life
x: Hun håpet å møte ham igjen hisset.

det Store, som her blot stykkevis og kjæmpende blev aabenbaret, det vil hisset samle sig til herlig Mening
The greatness which here was revealed only piecemeal and through struggle will in the hereafter come together into glorious meaning.

23655.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂éd
Probably derived from Old Norse hizi (“there”), also hize, compounded with at (“to, toward; at”). The latter is from Proto-Germanic *at (“at, toward, to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”). The first element is traditionally connected with the deictic family represented by hin (“that, yonder”).
The spatial sense “there, yonder” was extended figuratively and especially religiously to “in the hereafter”, contrasting life here with existence beyond death. hist (“yonder; in the hereafter”) is a contracted form of hisset; the Bokmål form hist was transmitted through Danis

a male given name from Hebrew, equivalent to English Jacob, a spelling variant of Jakob

1000295.etyen:
A spelling variant of Jakob, retaining the c found in Latin Iacobus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), from Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿăqōḇ). The meaning is disputed: the Old Testament associates the name with “holding the heel”, while another interpretation is “may God protect”. The surname is derived from the given name.
Compare Danish Jacob, Swedish Jacob, German Jacob, English Jacob and Czech Jakub (“male given names”).

[…] ginger, paprika powder, apple cider vinegar, yeast extract, elephant garlic, garlic, chilli powder […]

1005159.etyen:
Compound of jumbo (“jumbo, very large”) + hvitløk (“garlic”), literally “jumbo garlic”.
The first element ultimately comes from English jumbo (“large person, animal or thing”), of uncertain further origin. The second contains hvit (“white”), from Old Norse hvítr (“white”), from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz (“white”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt- (“to shine”), and løk (“onion”), from Old Norse laukr (“leek, onion, garlic”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laukaz (“leek, onion”), of uncertain further origin.
Compare the parallel formation Swedish jumbovitlök (“elephant garlic”).
